intro/hello: Welcome to the last lecture of the 2016 course. It points in two directions at once.
intro/time: The first is time. A video is a stack of images, so the question becomes where a ConvNet should mix different moments.
intro/labels: The second is learning without labels. Every network so far needed people to label thousands of examples.
intro/free: But unlabeled photos and videos are nearly free. Can we learn from them alone?
intro/ae: You will meet three ideas. Autoencoders squeeze their input into a small code, then rebuild it.
intro/vae: Variational autoencoders make that code something you can sample, to generate new data.
intro/gan: And generative adversarial networks pit a generator against a critic.
fusion/array: A color video clip is a four dimensional array: T frames, each an image of three by H by W numbers.
fusion/task: The classic task is action recognition: given a clip, say what is happening, like juggling.
fusion/data: Benchmarks included U C F one oh one, thirteen thousand clips of a hundred and one actions, and Sports one M, a million YouTube sports videos.
fusion/before: Before ConvNets, the best systems tracked many points through the video, and described the motion around each track: dense trajectories.
fusion/where: Can a ConvNet learn such features instead? And where in the network should the frames meet?
fusion/single: Karpathy and colleagues compared four answers. Single frame: an ordinary ConvNet on one frame, blind to time.
fusion/late: Late fusion runs the same network on two frames fifteen apart, and compares them only at the top.
fusion/early: Early fusion stacks ten frames as thirty input channels, so the first filters see them all, but only once.
fusion/slow: Slow fusion uses 3-D convolutions that merge a few neighboring moments at each layer.
fusion/result: The result was humbling: single frame was already strong, and slow fusion won by only a point or two.
fusion/why: Much of a sport shows in one frame: a pool, a ring, a pitch. Still, slow fusion's building block deserves a closer look.
conv3d/recall: A 2-D convolution slides a small filter over the rows and columns of an image, multiplying and adding at every spot.
conv3d/block: A 3-D convolution also slides along time. The filter is a little block: a few frames deep, and three by three in space.
conv3d/sum: Each output is the filter times the video block under it, summed: the 2-D loop, plus one loop for time.
conv3d/square: Here is a tiny video: a bright square that moves one pixel right on every frame.
conv3d/diff: Give the filter a weight of minus one on one frame and plus one on the next. It measures how much each pixel brightened.
conv3d/edges: Slide it through time. The output glows orange at the square's leading edge, and blue at its trailing edge. The filter sees motion.
conv3d/depth1: Make the filter one frame deep, and there is nothing to compare: the output is just a blurred copy, blind to motion.
conv3d/shrink: The output also has eight minus t plus one frames: deeper filters shorten a clip, as wider ones shrink an image.
conv3d/c3d: C 3 D, in 2015, took this all the way: a deep, V G G style network built only from three by three by three convolutions.
conv3d/features: Its features, fed to a linear classifier, worked well across many video tasks.
streams/route: Simonyan and Zisserman took another route: instead of hoping a network learns motion, feed it motion.
streams/flow: Optical flow says how far each pixel moved between two frames: two numbers per pixel, a horizontal and a vertical step.
streams/spatial: Their network has two streams. The spatial stream, an ordinary ConvNet on one color frame, sees appearance.
streams/temporal: The temporal stream sees motion: the flow of ten frames, stacked as twenty channels.
streams/avg: At the end, their class scores are averaged.
streams/surprise: Surprisingly, motion alone beat appearance. Together they reached about eighty eight percent on U C F one oh one, edging out the best hand designed features.
streams/short: Still, a 3-D ConvNet or a flow stack covers well under a second, and many events last much longer.
streams/lstm: So run a ConvNet on every frame, and feed the feature vectors, in order, into an L S T M.
streams/carry: Its memory spans the whole video, and its final state gives one label for all of it.
streams/rconv: Ballas and colleagues went further: a G R U whose matrix multiplies are convolutions, so the memory is itself a feature map.
streams/mix: In practice, the best systems combined these ideas.
unlabeled/sofar: So far, everything has been supervised: data x comes with labels y, and we learn to map one to the other.
unlabeled/cost: Labels are the expensive part. Someone looked at every one of ImageNet's million training images.
unlabeled/unsup: Unsupervised learning gets only the data, and looks for structure in it.
unlabeled/kinds: Clusters, a few directions that explain most of the variation, useful features, or how probable each point is.
unlabeled/feat: The 2016 lecture focused on two kinds. First, learning features: a compact code for each input, useful later.
unlabeled/gen: Second, generative models: learn the data's distribution well enough to make new samples.
autoencoder/idea: An autoencoder is a network trained to reproduce its own input, through a bottleneck.
autoencoder/enc: An encoder squeezes the input x into a small code z.
autoencoder/dec: A decoder expands z back into a reconstruction, x hat. The code is too small to copy x, so it must capture what matters most.
autoencoder/loss: The loss is the squared difference between input and output. No labels needed: the input is its own target.
autoencoder/toy: Here is the smallest version: points on an arc, each squeezed through a single number.
autoencoder/curve: The purple curve is all the decoder can make as z sweeps its range. Gray lines join each point to its reconstruction.
autoencoder/linear: A linear encoder and decoder can only make a straight line.
autoencoder/pca: Training finds the best line, the first principal component, just as P C A would. On an arc, most points end up far from home.
autoencoder/nonlin: Now give both a hidden layer of sixteen tan h units, and train again.
autoencoder/bend: The curve bends along the arc, and the loss falls from zero point two six to zero point zero zero three.
autoencoder/keep: Afterward, the decoder is usually dropped. The encoder is a feature extractor learned without labels, ready to feed a classifier or start a supervised network.
autoencoder/history: From about 2006 to 2010, this was how deep networks were trained at all: one layer at a time, each learning to rebuild the layer below.
autoencoder/fell: With ray-loos, good initialization and batch norm, networks train from random weights, so this had faded by 2016.
autoencoder/noise: A denoising autoencoder corrupts the input and rebuilds the clean version, so the code must capture structure rather than memorize.
autoencoder/gaps: But a plain autoencoder cannot generate well. Its codes leave gaps, and a random code may decode to garbage.
vae/vae: A variational autoencoder, from Kingma and Welling in 2014, turns this into a true generative model.
vae/story: Its story of how data is made: pick a code z at random from a standard bell curve, centered at zero with a spread of one. That bell is the prior.
vae/decode: Then decode it into a data point.
vae/easy: If that story produces realistic data, generating is easy: sample, then decode.
vae/encoder: Training also needs the reverse: from a data point to the codes that could have made it. That is the encoder's job.
vae/dist: It outputs a whole distribution: a mean, mu, and a spread, sigma, for each code number.
vae/give: Not code zero point seven, but a code around zero point seven, give or take zero point one.
vae/logvar: It predicts the log of sigma squared, since a network output can be any number, but a spread must be positive.
vae/coin: Training samples a code from that bell. But you cannot backpropagate through a coin flip.
vae/trick: The reparameterization trick: draw plain noise, epsilon, from the standard bell, stretch it by sigma, then shift it by mu.
vae/grads: Same bell, but now z is a smooth function of mu and sigma: nudge either, and every sample slides along. Gradients flow.
kl/loose: One more ingredient keeps the codes organized. Left alone, the encoder would shrink every sigma, and scatter the centers.
kl/gaps: Then random codes from the prior would land in empty gaps again.
kl/kl: So the loss also charges each encoder bell for differing from the prior, using the Kullback Leibler divergence, or K L.
kl/kldef: It measures how different two distributions are. It is never negative, and zero only when they match.
kl/closed: For two bells it has a short formula: half of mu squared, plus sigma squared, minus one, minus the log of sigma squared.
kl/mu: The mu squared term charges for a center away from zero.
kl/sigma: The rest charges for a spread other than one. It grows whether sigma shrinks or grows.
kl/fill: So every bell is pulled toward the prior. Codes overlap and fill it with no gaps, and a random code decodes to something sensible.
kl/elbo: Together, the V A E maximizes a lower bound on how probable it finds the data: the evidence lower bound.
kl/terms: Flip the sign, and the loss is a reconstruction error plus the K L penalty.
kl/balance: One term wants precise codes, the other wants codes that look like the prior. Their balance trades sharpness for organization.
vae-live/setup: Here is a tiny V A E on three hundred points along an arc, with a one number code.
vae-live/curve: The purple curve is the decoder's output across z, drawn darker where the prior is more likely.
vae-live/train: Each step encodes a batch, samples codes with the trick, decodes, and adds the two loss terms.
vae-live/along: Within a couple of thousand steps, the curve lies along the arc.
vae-live/gen: Now generate: decode two hundred codes drawn from the standard bell. The blue points are brand new data.
vae-live/cover: They cover the arc end to end, because the K L term made the codes fill the prior.
vae-live/blur: But they hug its middle and miss its thickness. Squared error rewards averaging plausible answers, which is why V A E images look blurry.
vae-live/faces: Real V A Es of the time made blurry but recognizable faces, and walking through z morphed one face smoothly into another.
gan/game: Generative adversarial networks, from Goodfellow and colleagues in 2014, skip probabilities altogether. Two networks play a game.
gan/G: A generator, G, turns random noise z into a sample, trying to make it look real.
gan/D: A discriminator, D, outputs the probability that a sample is real.
gan/clf: D trains as an ordinary classifier, with real samples labeled one and fakes zero. G trains to make D wrong.
gan/through: G never needs a formula for the data's probability. It learns only from how D reacts, by backpropagating through D.
gan/v1: Both goals fit in one number, the value. Its first term, the average of log D on real data, is high when D calls real data real...
gan/v2: and its second is high when D calls the fakes fake.
gan/minmax: D pushes the value up. G pushes it down.
gan/end: With unlimited capacity, the game ends with G matching the data, and D stuck at one half.
gan/flat: One practical fix matters. Early on, D easily rejects G's fakes, and the log of one minus D is nearly flat there: almost no gradient.
gan/ns: So G maximizes the log of D of G of z instead. Same goal, but a strong gradient exactly when G is bad.
gan/slopes: At zero point zero five, the old slope is about minus one. The new one is minus twenty.
gan-live/setup: Here it is on the smallest problem: real data are single numbers, drawn from two bumps.
gan-live/nets: G maps one random number to one sample. D maps one number to a probability.
gan-live/alt: Training alternates: a step on D with G frozen, then a step on G with D frozen.
gan-live/dmove: D, in gold, rises where fakes are too few, and dips where they pile up.
gan-live/gmove: G then shifts its samples toward what D likes.
gan-live/jump: Below is G itself. To turn one bell into two bumps, it must learn a steep jump in the middle.
gan-live/done: After four thousand rounds, the samples sit on both bumps, and D hovers near one half.
gan-live/reseed: But runs differ. Here is the same code, from another random seed.
gan-live/collapse: The generator collapses onto one bump, since those samples fool D for now. This is mode collapse.
gan-live/recover: This run recovers. Others oscillate, or settle on bumps of the wrong size.
gan-live/hard: With two networks chasing each other, neither loss says much about quality. In 2016, people coped with careful rules and by watching samples.
dcgan/fragile: Early image GANs were small and fragile. D C GAN, by Radford and colleagues in 2015, found rules that made them train reliably.
dcgan/rules: No pooling: strided convolutions in D, transpose convolutions to upsample in G. Batch norm in both, and no fully connected hidden layers.
dcgan/acts: Ray-loo in G with tan h at the output, and leaky ray-loo in D.
dcgan/results: It made convincing sixty four by sixty four bedrooms and faces.
dcgan/walk: Its latent space acted like a coordinate system: walk between two codes, and a TV slowly turns into a window.
dcgan/arith: Even arithmetic worked: average codes for smiling women, minus neutral women, plus neutral men...
dcgan/glasses: Man with glasses, minus man, plus woman, gives a woman with glasses.
dcgan/hybrids: Others followed: lap GAN built images coarse to fine, and hybrids put a GAN critic on a V A E to sharpen it.
outro/video: To recap: video asks where to mix time. Fusion, 3-D convolutions, optical flow, or a recurrent net on top.
outro/ae: Autoencoders learn without labels, by compressing and rebuilding.
outro/vae: V A Es sample their code with the reparameterization trick, and a K L penalty lets random codes decode to new data.
outro/gan: GANs pit a generator against a critic: sharp samples, unstable training.
outro/next: The three models all learn from the data itself, with no labels at all. That is where much of the field went next.
outro/dl26: The D L twenty six course carries the story on from here, with contrastive learning and diffusion models.
